analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment managers' profit shares as ordinary income instead of at the lower capital-gains rate.
analysis.headline: The Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2015, with 58 cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships are paid largely through "carried interest" — a share of the fund's profits — which under current law is taxed at the long-term capital-gains rate (top 20%) rather than as ordinary salary (top 39.6%). This bill would reclassify that profit share as ordinary income, apply payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare to it, and impose a 40% penalty on underpayments that use avoidance schemes. Genuine capital the manager actually invested would keep capital-gains treatment. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; it expired at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, whose tax burden would shift down slightly as high-earning fund managers lose a preferential rate and pay their share of Social Security and Medicare taxes; the added revenue could reduce deficits or fund priorities. Workers and salaried professionals who pay full ordinary rates on their income also gain a more even tax code.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats the net capital gain from an "investment services partnership interest" — a fund manager's carried interest — as ordinary income, closing the gap between the top 20% capital-gains rate and the top 39.6% wage rate [S2][S3].
It adds carried-interest income to self-employment earnings, so managers pay Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes on it like other workers do on their wages [S2][S3].
It raises the penalty on underpayments from 20% to 40% when taxpayers misclassify carried-interest income to avoid the new rules [S3].

It protects genuine capital: income from a "qualified capital interest" — money the manager actually invested, allocated the same way as outside investors' money — keeps capital-gains treatment, and certain family partnerships get an exemption [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate fund managers whose performance-based profit shares would be taxed at ordinary income rates plus self-employment tax, cutting their after-tax earnings substantially. Investment partnerships would face new reporting and recordkeeping requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The line between a manager's labor and their genuine capital investment is hard to draw: the bill's qualified-capital-interest exemption, family-partnership carve-out, and anti-abuse regulation authority (including rules to prevent avoidance through qualified family partnerships) create significant complexity and opportunities for structuring around the rules [S3].

Critics argue carried interest is a real return on risky invested capital, not salary, and that taxing it as ordinary income — including a self-employment tax on investment returns — misclassifies it and could discourage risk-taking in businesses like real estate development that the bill's definition of specified assets reaches (real estate held for rental or investment) [S3].

The bill's own structure acknowledges the compliance burden: it requires new reporting and recordkeeping systems for partnerships and grants the Treasury Secretary broad discretion to write regulations covering tiered partnerships, controlled groups of entities, and indirect dispositions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforwardly a fairness measure: it subjects one occupation's main form of pay to the same rates other workers pay on wages, while grandfathering genuine invested capital. The honest objections are practical — distinguishing labor returns from capital returns is genuinely hard, the compliance regime is heavy, and some real-estate and family investment structures get carve-outs that complicate the base. But the costs fall narrowly on a small set of very high earners, while the benefit — more even taxation and added revenue — is broad. On balance the benefit outweighs the cost; the bill's failure was a matter of committee inaction, not a floor vote on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sander Levin (D-MI) introduced the bill on June 25, 2015, joined by Reps. Van Hollen, Rangel, McDermott, and Ellison as original cosponsors [S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred [S5].
It attracted 58 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat [S4].
No version of the bill ever received a vote in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers, who kept paying the lower capital-gains rate on carried interest; no tax-writing action occurred during the Congress, and the preferential treatment continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping the tax break

for.name: Rep. Sander Levin (D-MI)
for.role: Sponsor; senior member of Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 58 cosponsors, all from his own party [S3][S4].

for.name: Reps. Van Hollen, Rangel, McDermott, and Ellison
for.what_they_did: Joined Levin in introducing the bill on the day it was filed [S3].

for.name: 58 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (under Chairman Paul Ryan, R-WI)
against.role: Committee of referral; sole gatekeeper for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — on the bill during the entire 114th Congress [S5].

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Largest financial beneficiary of carried-interest treatment
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years against changes to carried-interest taxation during the Obama administration's parallel push to close the loophole.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never brought the bill to a vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their main form of compensation — carried interest taxed at the 20% capital-gains rate — would be taxed as ordinary income up to 39.6% plus self-employment tax. Their gain under current law is a lower rate on pay that other professionals cannot get on wages [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Real estate investment and development partnerships
industries.note: Real estate held for rental or investment is a specified asset, so performance-based promotes in real estate deals would be recharacterized as ordinary income. Developers' after-tax returns on syndicated deals would fall [S3].

The bill exempts qualified family partnerships from part of the recharacterization rules, letting allocations to related family members count toward the capital-interest exemption — a carve-out other fund structures do not get [S3].
